ap.title: The Origins of the Modern Olympic Games
ap.passage:
The modern Olympic Games trace their origins to the efforts of a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin, who in the late nineteenth century sought to revive the ancient Greek tradition of athletic competition as a means of promoting international peace and cultural exchange. The first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896, featuring athletes from just fourteen nations competing in a limited number of events.

Coubertin believed that competitive sport could serve a purpose beyond simple entertainment, fostering mutual understanding and respect among nations whose relationships were often strained by political rivalry. This philosophy, sometimes referred to as Olympism, emphasized the value of participation and fair competition over the pursuit of victory alone.

Over the following century, the Games expanded dramatically in scale, eventually growing to include thousands of athletes representing well over one hundred countries and encompassing dozens of distinct sports. The Winter Olympics were introduced in 1924, providing a dedicated venue for snow and ice sports that had not been well accommodated within the original summer format.

Despite occasional disruptions caused by world wars, political boycotts, and, more recently, global health crises, the Olympic Games have remained a consistent symbol of international cooperation and athletic achievement. Modern host cities continue to invest enormous resources into hosting the event, viewing it as an opportunity to showcase their culture and infrastructure to a worldwide audience.

ctw.paragraph: The Earth's outer shell is divided into several large sections known as tectonic plates that move slowly across the planet's surface. Where two plates collide directly against each other, tremendous pressure builds up gradually until it is eventually released, often generating powerful earthquakes. In other locations, plates slide past one another horizontally along transform boundaries, creating a different but equally significant type of geological stress. When plates instead move apart from each other, molten material rises upward from beneath the surface, gradually forming new crust along the resulting gap. Understanding these different boundary types has proven essential for predicting where earthquakes and volcanic activity are most likely to occur.

ap.title: Plant Responses to Herbivory
ap.passage:
Plants, despite lacking the ability to flee from predators, have evolved a remarkable array of defenses against herbivorous insects and animals seeking to consume their tissues. These defenses range from physical barriers, such as thorns and tough leaf surfaces, to sophisticated chemical strategies that actively deter or harm potential attackers.

Among the most fascinating plant defenses are induced responses, in which a plant only produces certain defensive chemicals after detecting actual damage from herbivore feeding. When an insect begins chewing on a leaf, the plant can detect specific chemical compounds present in the insect's saliva, triggering a rapid increase in the production of toxic or unpalatable compounds throughout the affected tissue.

Some plant species have taken this defensive strategy even further, releasing volatile chemical signals into the air when attacked that can be detected by nearby plants of the same or even different species. These airborne signals appear to prompt neighboring plants to preemptively boost their own chemical defenses, even before they themselves have been attacked.

Certain plants have also evolved indirect defenses that recruit natural enemies of the herbivores attacking them. Some species release specific volatile compounds when damaged that attract predatory insects or parasitic wasps, which then attack the herbivores responsible for the damage, effectively turning the plant's attacker's own predators into unwitting allies.

ctw.paragraph: Procrastination is a remarkably common behavior that affects people across nearly every culture and profession. Contrary to popular belief, psychologists have found that procrastination is rarely caused simply by poor time management or laziness. Instead, researchers frequently identify underlying emotional factors, such as anxiety about failure or a strong desire for perfectionism, as significant contributors to chronic procrastination. Breaking large, intimidating tasks into smaller, more manageable steps has proven remarkably effective at reducing the emotional discomfort that often triggers procrastination in the first place. Understanding these psychological mechanisms has allowed researchers to develop targeted interventions that help people overcome persistent procrastination habits.

at.speaker: female
at.subject: Botany
at.transcript: Today's lecture covers seed dormancy, a fascinating survival strategy that allows seeds to delay germination until environmental conditions become favorable enough to support successful seedling growth. Without this mechanism, seeds might germinate immediately after forming, potentially during an unfavorable season, such as the onset of winter or the middle of an extended drought, resulting in near-certain failure for the resulting seedling before it could establish itself successfully. Plants have evolved several distinct mechanisms to enforce dormancy, and often use multiple mechanisms simultaneously for added reliability. Physical dormancy involves a seed coat that is impermeable to water, physically preventing the seed from absorbing the moisture it needs to begin germinating until that coat is sufficiently worn down or damaged, a process that can occur naturally through exposure to fluctuating soil temperatures, mechanical abrasion, or even passage through an animal's digestive system after the seed has been eaten and later excreted. Physiological dormancy, in contrast, involves internal chemical or hormonal factors within the seed itself, often requiring a specific extended period of cold temperatures, a process called stratification, before internal chemical changes occur that allow germination to proceed successfully. This particular adaptation ensures that seeds from many temperate plant species won't germinate immediately in autumn, right before winter arrives, but will instead wait until they've experienced a sufficient period of cold, ensuring germination occurs closer to the following spring instead, when growing conditions are considerably more favorable for a young seedling. Some seeds also exhibit a third type known as morphological dormancy, in which the embryo inside the seed simply hasn't finished developing at the time the seed disperses from the parent plant, requiring additional time for that embryo to mature further before it becomes physically capable of germinating at all. Understanding these varied dormancy mechanisms has significant practical importance for agriculture and horticulture, since farmers and gardeners often need to artificially break dormancy through specific techniques, such as deliberately scarifying tough seed coats or artificially cold-stratifying seeds, in order to reliably achieve successful and predictably timed germination for cultivated crops.

at.speaker: male
at.subject: Economics
at.transcript: Today we'll discuss the concept of comparative advantage, one of the foundational ideas underlying the modern economic case for international trade, first articulated in detail by the economist David Ricardo in the early nineteenth century. The theory begins with a seemingly counterintuitive insight: even if one country can produce absolutely every good more efficiently than another country, meaning it has an absolute advantage across the board, both countries can still benefit from trading with each other, provided each country specializes in producing whatever it can produce with the lowest relative opportunity cost compared to its other production options. To illustrate, imagine a scenario involving two countries and two goods, say wine and cloth. Even if one country is more efficient at producing both wine and cloth in absolute terms, it likely still has a relatively greater efficiency advantage in producing one of the two goods compared to the other, meaning the opportunity cost, in terms of the other good given up, of producing that particular good is comparatively lower for that country than for its trading partner. If each country specializes in producing the good for which it has the comparatively lower opportunity cost, and then trades with the other country for the good it did not produce, total combined global output of both goods increases, and both countries can end up consuming more of both goods than either could have achieved by trying to remain fully self-sufficient and produce everything domestically. This principle helps explain why international trade can generate genuine mutual economic benefit, even between countries with widely differing overall levels of productivity or economic development. It's worth noting, however, that comparative advantage as a theoretical model doesn't account for every real-world complication that can affect actual trade outcomes, including transportation costs, trade barriers such as tariffs, fluctuating exchange rates, and importantly, the uneven distribution of the resulting economic gains within each individual country, since certain domestic industries and workers may still be genuinely harmed by increased trade competition even while the country's economy benefits substantially in aggregate overall terms.

at.speaker: female
at.subject: Neuroscience
at.transcript: Today's lecture examines neuroplasticity, the brain's remarkable capacity to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout an individual's life, a discovery that fundamentally overturned an older scientific assumption that the adult brain's structure was essentially fixed and largely unchangeable after childhood development concluded. Neuroplasticity operates at multiple different levels within the nervous system. At the most fundamental level, synaptic plasticity refers to the strengthening or weakening of individual connections between neurons based on patterns of activity and actual usage, generally following a well-established principle often summarized by the phrase neurons that fire together wire together, meaning connections that are frequently and repeatedly activated tend to become progressively stronger over time, while connections that go largely unused tend to gradually weaken. This basic mechanism is now understood to underlie learning and memory formation at a fundamental biological level. At a somewhat larger structural scale, the brain can also demonstrate more significant structural reorganization in response to injury or considerable environmental change, with functions sometimes shifting to entirely different brain regions when the areas originally responsible for those functions become damaged. This capacity for reorganization has proven especially significant for stroke rehabilitation, since patients who have experienced localized brain damage can sometimes recover meaningful lost function as neighboring or entirely different brain regions gradually take over responsibilities previously handled by the damaged tissue, particularly when patients engage consistently in intensive, targeted rehabilitative therapy following their injury. Interestingly, research has also demonstrated that neuroplasticity, while generally most pronounced and flexible during critical developmental periods in early childhood, nevertheless continues in a somewhat more limited capacity throughout adulthood as well. Studies of London taxi drivers, for example, famously found that these drivers, who must memorize the city's extraordinarily complex street layout in considerable detail, developed a measurably larger hippocampus, the brain region strongly associated with spatial memory and navigation, compared to individuals in various control groups, and this structural difference appeared to increase progressively the longer an individual had actively worked as a taxi driver.

at.speaker: male
at.subject: Archaeology
at.transcript: Today we'll look at the archaeological discovery and significance of Göbekli Tepe, a remarkable site in southeastern Turkey that has substantially challenged long-held assumptions about the sequence of early human social and technological development. Excavations at the site, which began in earnest during the nineteen nineties, revealed a complex of massive carved stone pillars, some standing over five meters tall and arranged in large circular enclosures, dating back roughly eleven thousand years, making it considerably older than previously known comparable monumental structures such as Stonehenge or even the earliest Egyptian pyramids, predating them by several thousand years. What makes Göbekli Tepe particularly significant is the timing of its construction relative to other major developments in human history. Conventional archaeological understanding had long assumed that large-scale monumental construction projects required first having a settled agricultural society, since farming was thought necessary to reliably generate the surplus food required to support the specialized non-farming labor needed for such ambitious large-scale building projects. However, evidence strongly suggests that the people who constructed Göbekli Tepe were still primarily hunter-gatherers, since clear evidence of systematic agriculture in the surrounding region doesn't appear in the archaeological record until somewhat later. This finding has led some researchers to propose a genuinely provocative alternative hypothesis: rather than agriculture necessarily enabling monumental construction and organized religious activity, perhaps the organizational and social demands of building and maintaining a large, significant ceremonial site like Göbekli Tepe actually helped drive the eventual development and adoption of agriculture in the surrounding region, as large groups of people gathering periodically for construction and ceremonial purposes would have required increasingly reliable food sources to sustain themselves during their time at the site. This hypothesis remains genuinely debated among archaeologists, but the site has nonetheless prompted a broader ongoing reconsideration of the traditional assumed relationship between agriculture, religion, and complex social organization in the story of early human civilization.

email.scenario: You ordered a textbook online for your course, but the wrong edition arrived. You need the correct edition before your exam next week and want to request an exchange.
email.subject: Received wrong textbook edition

tasks.description: Explain that you received the wrong edition of the textbook.
Mention that you need the correct edition before your exam.
Request an exchange for the correct edition.

email.exampleResponse:
Dear Customer Support,

I recently ordered the textbook for my chemistry course, but the fourth edition arrived instead of the fifth edition I actually need.

My exam is next week, so I need the correct edition as soon as possible.

Could you please arrange an exchange and send the fifth edition right away? I am happy to return the incorrect copy using a prepaid label if needed. Thank you for your quick attention to this.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

disc.subject: environmental science
disc.prompt: We've been discussing whether cities should ban single-use plastic bags entirely. Some argue a full ban is necessary to meaningfully reduce plastic pollution, while others argue that a small fee on plastic bags is more practical and achieves similar results without inconveniencing shoppers. Should cities implement a full ban on single-use plastic bags? Why or why not?

classmates.name: Naomi
classmates.opinion: I support a full ban. A small fee still allows people who can afford it to keep using plastic bags without much thought, which limits how much actual behavior change occurs. A full ban forces everyone to adapt, which is uncomfortable at first but leads to much larger reductions in plastic waste over time.

classmates.name: Tomas
classmates.opinion: I think a fee is the better approach. It still reduces usage significantly, since research shows even small fees discourage a lot of people, but it avoids penalizing situations where someone genuinely forgot a reusable bag. A full ban can feel overly restrictive and creates enforcement headaches for small businesses that a fee doesn't.

disc.exampleResponse: The debate between a full plastic bag ban and a small fee comes down to weighing effectiveness against practicality. Naomi makes a compelling point that a fee alone may not push everyone toward meaningful change, since people who can easily afford it might not adjust their behavior much. At the same time, Tomas raises a fair concern about flexibility for occasional situations, and about the burden a ban could place on smaller businesses trying to enforce it. Personally, I lean toward agreeing with Naomi that a full ban produces a larger overall impact, though I think cities could ease the transition by providing free reusable bags to lower-income households during the initial rollout, addressing some of Tomas's concerns about fairness without abandoning the stronger environmental benefits of a full ban.

interview.speaker: female
interview.introText: You have agreed to take part in a research study about attitudes toward city living. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.text: Thank you for joining me today. Let's begin with something simple. Do you prefer living in a big city or a smaller town, and why?
I see. What do you think is the biggest advantage of living in a big city?
That's a good point. And what would you say is the biggest drawback of city living?
Great, one last question. Do you think cities are doing enough to remain affordable for young people? Why or why not?
